titre: Putting Nine Hundred Tombs in Order Without Any Scale of Years
accroche: In 1901, Petrie sorts Egyptian tombs by their pottery and numbers the stages from 30 to 80. These numbers are not years.
contenu_vulgarise:
Hundreds of tombs, thousands of pots, and not a single king's name to say which comes before which. In 1895, Flinders Petrie excavates at Naqada, in Egypt, a cemetery of about 2,200 predynastic tombs. He needs an order.

## One card per tomb

Until then, he points out, prehistoric periods had been named after the places where they were best represented (the Chellean, the Mousterian, the Hallstattian), and all one could say was that one preceded another. A system he considers cumbersome and imprecise.

He details his method in 1901 in the Diospolis Parva report, devoted to the cemeteries of Abadiyeh and Hu. First he numbers all the pottery forms. Then, on one strip of cardboard per tomb, he notes the numbers of the forms found, in nine columns, one for each kind of pottery. Each tomb becomes a row of figures that can be compared at a glance with any other.

## The shortest spread

The strips remain to be arranged. The principle is simple: a type of pot appears, lasts, disappears. If the order is the right one, each type occupies the smallest possible span; any disorder can only stretch it out. Petrie pulls on this criterion like on elastic threads: each type is a thread attached to all the strips that contain it, and the probable position of each strip is the one it takes under the tension of all these threads. He adds a reading of the plausibility of styles that he calls “artistic and subjective,” but specifies that it must never override the statistical facts.

The order thus obtained has no meaning yet: we do not know which end is the oldest. That is given by the contents of the wavy-handled jars. These jars go from an almost spherical form to a narrow cylinder, the handle shrinking to a wavy line. The earliest contain an aromatic ointment, the next a layer of clay over the ointment, the last solid clay. For Petrie, this degradation of the contents into a worthless substitute proves which way the changes run.

## Numbers, not years

About 700 strips are sorted at first, then 900 in the final version, and divided into 50 equal groups, numbered from 30 to 80. He starts at 30 to leave room for older periods that might be found, and stops at 80 to keep numbers up to 100 for linking up with written history.

He writes that these numbers are “purely arbitrary” and that each number represents an equal quantity of tombs. A number is therefore not a duration: stage 45 is not located fifteen years after stage 30. The scale gives a before and an after, with a precision that period names did not have, and that is all it promises. A new tomb, as long as it contains pottery, can be read into it at once.

The result has endured: according to the Whipple Library at Cambridge, it was the first time Egyptologists dated prehistoric sites by pottery alone, and they still use its predynastic chronology. What remains is the question this scale does not ask: how many years separate stage 35 from stage 65?

repere.texte: Petrie divides 900 cardboard strips, one per tomb, into 50 equal groups numbered from 30 to 80. These numbers are, he writes, “purely arbitrary”: each represents an equal quantity of tombs, not a number of years.
repere.source: W. M. Flinders Petrie, Diospolis Parva: The Cemeteries of Abadiyeh and Hu, 1898-9, Egypt Exploration Fund, London, 1901, pp. 4–8

carte.punch: Petrie arranged 900 tombs with no scale of years: he gave them an order.
carte.idee: In 1901, Petrie arranges 900 Egyptian tombs by their pottery and numbers the stages from 30 to 80. Each number groups as many tombs as the others: it is a rank, not a number of years.

quiz.question: How does Petrie determine which end of his series of tombs is the oldest?
choix: By the depth at which each tomb was dug into the cemetery floor
By the degradation of the contents of the wavy-handled jars, from ointment to clay
By the names of kings engraved on objects in the tombs presumed to be the most recent
By comparison with prehistoric periods in Europe, such as the Mousterian or the Hallstattian
quiz.explication: The order of the tombs comes from the distribution of pottery types; the direction comes from the contents of the wavy-handled jars: aromatic ointment, then clay over ointment, then solid clay, a worthless substitute that can only come later. Kings' names are precisely what these pre-writing tombs lack, and periods named after places are the system Petrie found cumbersome.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does each numbered stage from 30 to 80 represent in Petrie's chronology?
choix: A century, estimated by comparison with the dates of written history
A royal dynasty known from tomb inscriptions
A group of tombs, as numerous as in the others
A layer of earth identified by its depth in the ground
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Petrie divides his strips into 50 equal groups: each number represents an equal quantity of tombs, not a number of years. No inscription or depth measurement enters into the definition of the stages.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Petrie's scale start at 30 and stop at 80?
choix: Because the first thirty tombs excavated were empty and had no pottery
Because numbers below thirty were reserved for stone vessels
Because Petrie wanted the scale to land on round dates in years
To leave room for older periods and then link up with written history
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Petrie explains that older periods might still be discovered, hence the start at 30, and that numbers had to remain free before 100 to link up with historical times. The numbers themselves are arbitrary: round-number years and empty tombs play no role in them.
